title: Triangulation
summary: Lose a move on purpose, with the king on a triangle, so that the opponent is left with the wrong side to move.
part.zugzwang.title: Zugzwang
part.zugzwang.summary: The position is great, but it is your move, and chess has no pass.
step.t_zugzwang: The kings face each other, and the c6-pawn is protected by my king. It is Black to move. Where can the black king go, and what does my king do in each case?
step.t_zugzwang.hint1: Count the black king's squares. The c6-pawn covers two of them, and the white king covers others.
step.t_zugzwang.hint2: Only three squares are left, all on the eighth rank. For each one, see which square on the sixth rank the black king stops watching.
step.zugzwang: With Black to move, it is over. The black king cannot go to b7 or d7, which the c6-pawn covers, nor to b6 or d6, next to my king. That leaves b8, c8 and d8, and from any of them he opens the door: my king goes to b6 or d6, wins the a6-pawn or walks the c6-pawn home. That is zugzwang: having to move is the misfortune.
step.pass: Now the same position with White to move. My king cannot go to b6 or d6, next to the black king, and b5 is covered by the a6-pawn. After 1.Kb4, 1.Kc4 or 1.Kd4, the c6-pawn falls. Only 1.Kd5 still protects it, and from there my king has to come back to c5 with the right side to move. I would love to say "pass", but chess does not allow it. So I will lose a move some other way: that is what this lesson is about.
step.d_zugzwang: First look at the prize: the position with Black to move. I play both sides.
step.d_zugzwang.m1: 1...Kc8. Any square of the black king opens a door; he picks c8, and b6 is free.
step.d_zugzwang.m2: 2.Kb6. My king goes in. From here it attacks a6 and watches b7 and c7.
step.d_zugzwang.m3: 2...Kd8. The black king stays near c7 to slow the pawn down.
step.d_zugzwang.m4: 3.Kb7: now c8 is mine too. The c6-pawn has a free road.
step.d_zugzwang.m5: 3...Ke7. He tries to reach d6 to attack the pawn from behind.
step.d_zugzwang.m6: 4.c7. The pawn advances protected by my king on b7, and c8 is mine.
step.d_zugzwang.m7: 4...Kd6. The black king attacks c7, but the pawn is protected, and c8 is out of his reach.
step.d_zugzwang.m8: 5.c8=Q. All because Black had the move.
step.zzMove: The black king is on c7 and yours on d5. Put Black in zugzwang, then go in.
step.zzMove.hint: Put your king face to face with the black king, without letting go of the c6-pawn. Then go in on the a6-pawn side.
step.zzMove.done: That's it. 1.Kc5 left Black with the move, the white king got to b6 and the a6-pawn fell. Two pawns up, the rest is technique.
part.triangle.title: The triangle
part.triangle.summary: Three neighbouring squares, three moves, and the same position comes back with Black to move.
step.t_triangle: This is the key position of the lesson. You want the zugzwang position from the first chapter, but with Black to move. How do you get there?
step.t_triangle.hint1: Compare the two kings' squares. Where can the white king walk without letting go of the c6-pawn? And the black king, without letting go of c8?
step.t_triangle.hint2: Count the squares from which your king still protects the c6-pawn and that touch each other. Now count the squares the black king has near c8.
step.t_triangle.hint3: A round trip over three squares takes three moves. Over two squares, it takes two. Who arrives late?
step.pairs: Think in pairs. White king on c5 and black king on c7, Black to move: zugzwang, you have seen it. The same holds for d6 against d8, and for d5 against c8. These squares correspond: when my king stands on one, the black king must stand on the other, with me to move. Here we have d5 against c8, and it is my move. The right pair with the wrong turn.
step.why: The cleanest way out is the triangle. My king goes from d5 to c4, from c4 to d4, and from d4 back to d5: three moves, and at the end d5 guards the pawn again. The black king would like to do the same, but he cannot: b7 and d7 are covered by the c6-pawn, and c7 is a poisoned square, because there he attacks the pawn, but my king returns to c5 or d5 and it is his move. That leaves c8, d8 and b8, where he can only swing back and forth in twos. Three moves against two: at the end of the trip, he is the one to move.
step.d_triangle.m1: 1.Kc4, the first corner. The c6-pawn is safe: on c8, the black king cannot reach it.
step.d_triangle.m2: 1...Kd8. The black king waits. On c7 he would fall into zugzwang after 2.Kc5, and d7 is covered by the pawn.
step.d_triangle.m3: 2.Kd4, the second corner. From here my king can still go back to c5 or d5, and from d8 the black king cannot reach the c6-pawn.
step.d_triangle.m4: 2...Kc8. He goes back to c8: he has no third square to make a triangle of his own.
step.d_triangle.m5: 3.Kd5, and the trip is complete: the starting position, now with Black to move.
step.d_triangle.m6: 3...Kc7. The black king attacks c6, but c7 is the poisoned square.
step.d_triangle.m7: 4.Kc5. My king protects c6, and this is the zugzwang from the first chapter, now with Black to move. Next, my king goes in on b6 or d6.
step.triangleMove: Make the triangle and come back to d5 with Black to move.
step.triangleMove.hint: Walk round two squares behind d5 and come back. When the black king attacks the pawn, stand face to face with it.
step.triangleMove.done: Perfect. Three moves to get back to d5, and the black king, with two squares, arrived late. Now he is in zugzwang.
part.detour.title: The longer way
part.detour.summary: To reach a square with the right side to move, the king uses two sides of the triangle instead of one.
step.t_detour: In the previous chapter the king walked round and came back to the same square. Now it wants to reach a new square. The pawns are blocked on d5 and d6: my king wants to capture the one on d6, the black king wants to capture the one on d5. My king's natural attacking square is e6. How do you get there without handing the move to the black king?
step.t_detour.hint1: Imagine your king on e6 and the black king on c5. Whoever has the move loses his pawn.
step.t_detour.hint2: If you go straight to e6, the black king reaches his square too, and the move is yours.
step.t_detour.hint3: Reach e6 in two moves instead of one, via a square that also touches e6.
step.detour: White king on e6 and black king on c5: each protects his own pawn and attacks the other one. Whoever has to move lets go of his pawn or of the attack, and loses. It is a mutual zugzwang. So e6 is only good if I get there with Black to move.
step.detourWrong: The natural move is 1.Ke6? But the black king answers 1...Kc5! Now I am the one who has to move: after 2.Kf5, for example, 2...Kxd5 follows, and Black is the one who wins. One move too few on the way, and the zugzwang turned against me.
step.d_detour: Now the right way. The squares f6, e7 and e6 form a triangle, and I use two of its sides instead of one.
step.d_detour.m1: 1.Ke7! The first side of the triangle. From here my king already attacks the d6-pawn, and the black king has to hurry to protect it.
step.d_detour.m2: 1...Kc5. The black king goes to his good square and protects d6. But he got there too early.
step.d_detour.m3: 2.Ke6. The second side. I reached e6 with Black to move: the mutual zugzwang, now against him.
step.d_detour.m4: 2...Kb5. Any black king move gives up the protection of d6.
step.d_detour.m5: 3.Kxd6. I captured the pawn, and mine, on d5, stays protected by the king.
step.d_detour.m6: 3...Kc4. The black king attacks d5, but the pawn is protected.
step.d_detour.m7: 4.Kc6. My king keeps protecting the pawn and controls d6 and d7, the squares in front of it: the road to the queen is open.
step.detourMove: Reach e6 with Black to move and capture the d6-pawn.
step.detourMove.hint: Do not go straight to the attacking square: get there in two moves.
step.detourMove.done: That's it. 1.Ke7 and 2.Ke6: two moves instead of one, and the black king was left with the move. When the right square is one step away, the shortest road is sometimes the wrong one.
part.kasparov.title: Black triangulates
part.kasparov.summary: Either side can triangulate. Kasparov did it with Black against Alburt, in 1978.
step.t_kasparov: {{Daugavpils|daugavpils}}, 1978, qualifying tournament for the {{Soviet Championship|soviet-championship}}: {{Lev Alburt|lev-alburt}}, with White, against the young {{Garry Kasparov|garry-kasparov}}. The queens came off, and in the pawn ending the kings marched up to here. Look at the white pawn on h3: Black wants to bring the king to g3 and capture it. When the position comes back with White to move, 58.Kf2 will be met by 58...Kf4, and the white king will have to give way. But right now it is Black to move. How does Black pass the move?
step.t_kasparov.hint1: Imagine White to move. The white king has little room: e2 and g2 are covered by the f3-pawn.
step.t_kasparov.hint2: Look for three neighbouring squares near e4 from which your king still watches f4.
step.kasparov: It is the problem of the key position, on the other side of the board and with the colours reversed. The f3-pawn covers e2 and g2, and the white king has little room. {{Kasparov|garry-kasparov}} played 55...Kf5 and, after 56.Kg1, 56...Ke5. {{Alburt|lev-alburt}} resigned, because after 57.Kf1 Ke4 the position comes back with White to move.
step.d_kasparov: The game, and what would have followed {{Alburt|lev-alburt}}'s resignation.
step.d_kasparov.m1: 55...Kf5. The first side of the triangle. From f5 the black king still watches f4 and can go back to e4.
step.d_kasparov.m2: 56.Kg1. If the white king stepped up to f2, the black king would face it on f4. He waits on g1.
step.d_kasparov.m3: 56...Ke5. The second side. Here {{Alburt|lev-alburt}} resigned; the rest is what would have followed.
step.d_kasparov.m4: 57.Kf1. The white king goes back to his starting square.
step.d_kasparov.m5: 57...Ke4. The third side: the starting position, now with White to move.
step.d_kasparov.m6: 58.Kf2. The white king tries to hold g3.
step.d_kasparov.m7: 58...Kf4. Opposition. The white king has to step aside, and the black king reaches g3 to capture the h3-pawn.
step.kasparovMove: Now you, with Black, in the game position. This time the white king tries another way.
step.kasparovMove.hint: Start with the triangle. If the white king steps up, stand face to face with it.
step.kasparovMove.done: Exactly. With 56.Kf2 White ran for the opposition, but it was his move: 56...Kf4 and 57...Kg3.
part.road.title: Before the triangle
part.road.summary: Before the triangle, the pawn walks with the king in front until you reach the position you know.
step.t_road: {{Kasparov|garry-kasparov}}'s position did not fall from the sky: two moves earlier, in the same game, he built it. You already know that with the pawn on f3, the black king on e4 and the white king on f1, Black wins. How do you take the f4-pawn to f3 without losing it?
step.t_road.hint1: A lone pawn on f3 falls: the white king captures it.
step.t_road.hint2: Before the pawn reaches f3, the black king has to stand next to it.
step.road: The plan is the pawn on f3 with the king on e4. {{Kasparov|garry-kasparov}} had already played 52...f4, which takes e3 and g3 away from the white king. Now the order matters: first the king goes to e4, and only then does the pawn step to f3, already protected.
step.d_road: The game moves, up to the position of the previous chapter.
step.d_road.m1: 53...Ke4! The king first. Now, when the pawn goes to f3, it will be protected.
step.d_road.m2: 54.Ke2. The white king faces the black one and watches f3.
step.d_road.m3: 54...f3+. The pawn reaches f3 with check, protected by the king.
step.d_road.m4: 55.Kf1. It is the position of the previous chapter, with Black to move. The triangle came from here.
step.roadWrong: And what if Black had played 53...f3? With the black king still on e5, 54.Kxf3 follows, and the lone pawn falls. What is left is rook pawn against rook pawn, and the white king protects the h3-pawn: a draw.
step.roadMove: Now you, with Black, two moves before {{Kasparov|garry-kasparov}}'s position. The white king will not play like {{Alburt|lev-alburt}}.
step.roadMove.hint: King first: bring it next to f3 before pushing the pawn.
step.roadMove.done: That's it. 53...Ke4 and, after 54.Kg2, 54...f3+: the pawn reached f3 protected by the king, and the white king, in check, has to move away. It is the road to the position of the previous chapter.
part.far.title: The triangle from afar
part.far.summary: With the kings six ranks apart, the count of squares is the same.
step.t_far: Until now the two kings fought over the same pawns. Now each one looks after a different group, far from the other. The white pawns on d6 and e7 tie the black king down: he cannot leave e8. The black pawns on g5 and h5 want to run, and my king, on g2, looks after them. If Black had the move, he would be lost. How do you pass the move to him?
step.t_far.hint1: Count the black king's squares: he only goes from e8 to d7 or f7 and back.
step.t_far.hint2: Black also has pawn moves to wait with. Look at what each of them does with your king on g3, f3 or h3.
step.t_far.hint3: You need to get back to g2 and pass the move: look for three neighbouring squares from which your king answers any pawn move.
step.far: If it were Black to move, the black king could not leave e8, and every pawn advance would have an answer: my king would stop in front of it. But it is my move. If I play 1.Kg3, Black answers 1...g4, and if I play 1.Kf3 or 1.Kh3, 1...h4 comes: each square of my king has the right pawn move, and it is a draw. So I make the triangle g2, h2, g3 and come back to g2 in three moves. This position comes from the analysis of a game {{Shirov|alexei-shirov}} against {{Grischuk|alexander-grischuk}}, {{New Delhi|new-delhi}}, 2000, here without the c-pawns.
step.d_far: Watch the trip, and what happens when Black is left with the move.
step.d_far.m1: 1.Kh2! From here my king goes to g3 or h3, depending on which pawn advances.
step.d_far.m2: 1...Kf7. The black king can only shuffle near e8.
step.d_far.m3: 2.Kg3. The second side of the triangle. With the black king on f7, no pawn move saves him.
step.d_far.m4: 2...Ke8. He goes back: there is nothing else to do.
step.d_far.m5: 3.Kg2. The starting position, now with Black to move.
step.d_far.m7: 4.Kg3. My king stops both pawns. Then it goes to collect them, and the black king, tied to e8, cannot help.
step.farMove: Pass the move to Black and stop the pawns.
step.farMove.hint: Come back to g2 via three neighbouring squares. When a black pawn advances, put your king in front of it.
step.farMove.done: Perfect. The black king is far away, but the count is the same: three moves against two.
part.defend.title: Defending from afar
part.defend.summary: From afar, the distant opposition answers every square of the attacker.
step.t_defend: Now you defend, and the kings are far from each other. The white king is looking for a way in and has plenty of squares to walk round. Where does the black king belong?
step.t_defend.hint1: When the kings are far apart, the defender's weapon is the one from the distant opposition lesson.
step.t_defend.hint2: Look at the white king's file and count the squares between the two kings.
step.defend: The triangle only works when the other king has no answer. Here Black has one: 1...Ke7! The kings stand on the same file with three squares between them: that is the distant opposition. The natural mistake is 1...Kf6? Then 2.Kf4 takes the opposition for White: after 2...Ke6 3.Ke4, the black king has to give way. The rule is to answer every square of the white king with the square that corresponds to it.
step.d_defend.m1: 1...Ke7! Same file, three squares between the kings.
step.d_defend.m3: 2...Kf6. The black king changes with it, and now the kings stand face to face.
step.d_defend.m5: 3...Ke6. Face to face again: the white king cannot get through the fifth rank.
step.d_defend.m6: 4.Kd3. He drops back to try the queenside.
step.d_defend.m7: 4...Kd7. Same file, three squares between them. Every white move has an answer.
step.defendMove: Answer every move of the white king.
step.defendMove.hint: Stay on the white king's file: from afar, with an odd number of squares between the kings; up close, face to face.
step.defendMove.done: Well done. The white king had squares to walk round, but each one had its answer. A draw.
step.recap: Three rules to take away. First: if the position is good but the turn is bad, lose a move with the triangle, three neighbouring squares and three moves to come back; and to reach a new square with the right side to move, use two sides of the triangle instead of one. Second: the triangle works with Black and from afar, and sometimes you have to steer the position into it, with the pawn walking behind the king. Third: the defender answers square by square; from afar, with the distant opposition.
step.finish: Now play the key position to the end. Triangle, zugzwang, and only then go in.
ex.e05: The advance with check is tempting. Find the winning move.
ex.e05.hint: After 1.c6+? the black king goes to c8 and draws. Look for a triangle around d5.
ex.e05.solution: 1.Ke5, 2.Kd4 and 3.Kd5: the triangle d5, e5, d4 gives back the position with Black to move. After 1...Kc6, 2.Kd4! is the only move. On the first move 1.Kc4, 1.Kd4 and 1.Ke4 also win; only 1.c6+? draws.
ex.e04: Attacking the f7-pawn looks obvious. Watch out for the turn. Find the winning move.
ex.e04.hint: The white king wants to be on g7 with Black to move. Get there another way.
ex.e04.solution: 1.Kg8! (1.Kh8 also wins). If 1...Ke6, 2.Kg7! and now the zugzwang is Black's: the black king has to let go of f7. 1.Kg7? straight away loses: after 1...Ke6 it is the white king that must leave g7, and the f6-pawn falls.
ex.e12: Attacking the d4-pawn with the king is the natural move. Is it the right one? Find the winning move.
ex.e12.hint: 1.Kc4? lets the black king into e4, and the d-pawn runs. King on d3 against king on e5 is reciprocal zugzwang: return to d3 in three moves.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Kd2! (1.Kc2 and 1.Ke2 also win) and, after 1...Kf6, 2.Ke2 and 3.Kd3: the same position with Black to move. The black king only has f6 and d6 to wait on, and any step away from e5 lets a white pawn advance: f6 or g5. 1.Kc4? Ke4! only draws: 2.f6 d3, 3.Kc3 Ke3, and both pawns promote.
ex.e10: Only one move keeps the win. Find the winning move.
ex.e10.hint: If it were Black to move in this very position, the black king would have to leave e4. Come back to e2 in three moves.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Ke1! and, after 1...Kf5, 2.Kd2 and 3.Ke2: the triangle e2, e1, d2, and the same position with Black to move. The black king only has f5 and the advance d4, and both lose. Any other first move draws.
ex.e16: The g6- and h5-pawns tie the black king down, but the e4-pawn wants to run. Only one move wins.
ex.e16.hint: The key position is king on f4 against king on f6, with the black pawn on d5: Black to move loses, White to move only draws. Reach f4 with the right turn: spend one move more on the way.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Kg4! Kf6 (everything loses) 2.Kg3! The king went from h3 to g3 in two moves instead of one, and now it is Black who has to move. If 2...d5, 3.Kf4! and the black king must give up f6 or the e4-pawn: 3...Kg7 4.Kxe4, or 3...Ke7 and the white king gets in via g5. If 2...e3, 3.Kf3 and the pawn falls with the black king still tied to g7 and f6. 1.Kg3? at once: 1...d5! 2.Kf4 Kf6, the same position with White to move, and it is a draw.
ex.e09: {{Grigoriev|nikolai-grigoriev}}'s study. The white king wants to reach e2, e3 or d4.
ex.e09.hint: The advance 1.d4? draws. The black king only has f3 and f4 to wait on; the white king has several squares behind. Take a walk.
ex.e09.solution: 1.Kc2, 2.Kb3, 3.Kb2 and 4.Kc2 again: the white king goes round and the black king, with only f3 and f4, arrives late. After 5.Kd2 and 5...Kf4, 6.Ke2! takes a key square. On the first move 1.d4? and 1.Ke1? draw; in the middle of the walk other king moves work too.
key.zugzwang: The position White wants: the kings face each other and Black is to move. The black king has to give way, and the white one walks in.
key.triangle: White has the right position but the wrong side to move. The white king walks round a triangle of three neighbouring squares; the black one, with only two squares to shuffle between, hands the move back.
key.alburtKasparov: {{Alburt|lev-alburt}} against {{Kasparov|garry-kasparov}}, 1978: the young {{Kasparov|garry-kasparov}} took his king on a three-move round trip, handed the move back to his opponent, and {{Alburt|lev-alburt}} resigned.
key.defend: The black king does not let the white one through: it always stays on the same file, at a distance that forces the white king to give way.
history: To triangulate is to lose a move on purpose. The king walks round three neighbouring squares, in a triangle, and comes back to where it was; the enemy king, with less room, cannot copy it, and ends up with the wrong side to move. Walking in a circle to get back to the same spot feels strange, which is why so many players miss the manoeuvre even with the win in hand. In 1978 the young {{Kasparov|garry-kasparov}} beat {{Lev Alburt|lev-alburt}} with a king triangle: he walked round, handed the move back to his opponent, and {{Alburt|lev-alburt}} resigned. The idea is not limited to pawn endings: at the 1965 {{Candidates|candidates}}, Spassky triangulated with his king in a rook ending against {{Tal|mikhail-tal}} and went on to play for the world title. {{Dvoretsky|mark-dvoretsky}} gave it its own section in his endgame manual.
practice: Now the real ending, from the start: king on c5 against king on c7, and it is your move. Only one move keeps the pawn. Find it, make the triangle and win. Choose the pace and go.
key.far: The white king is far away, but the idea is the same: a round trip over three squares passes the move to the black king, tied down near the white pawns.
